caps.t:
Seventeen astronauts have
died in three NASA disasters,

and before each one, the
danger was already on paper.

Each time, the person who gave
the warning lost the argument.

In July 2003, investigators fired a block
of foam at a real piece of shuttle wing,
at about five hundred miles an hour.
The foam weighed less than two pounds.

It left a hole about
sixteen inches across.

Six months earlier, foam like
that had hit the shuttle Columbia,

and engineers had asked for pictures of
the wing while the crew was still in orbit.
They didn't get them.

The first warnings NASA ignored were
written nearly forty years earlier,

about a capsule on a
launch pad in Florida.
On the afternoon of 27 January

1967, three men climbed into the first
Apollo capsule built to carry a crew,
on Launch Complex 34 at Cape Kennedy.

Gus Grissom had been the
second American in space,

and he was so fed up with the mismatch
between his simulator and the real spacecraft
that he had hung a lemon on the simulator.

Ed White had been the first
American to walk in space.

Roger Chaffee was getting
ready for his first flight.

It was a launch rehearsal, and the
rocket under them had no fuel in it.

The review board later found that neither
NASA nor the builder had classed the test
as hazardous.
The cabin was filled with pure oxygen,

pumped a little above the
pressure of the air outside.

In pure oxygen, things that barely
smoulder in normal air burn fast and hot.

Nobody had kept a close count of
what in that cabin could burn.

The hatch opened inward, so the
pressure inside held it shut,

and even under ideal conditions it
took at least ninety seconds to open.

A Senate committee later said the fire
hazards of pure oxygen were well documented,

yet NASA and the contractor
were completely unprepared.

Other warnings were about
the spacecraft itself.

In late 1965, a review led by
the Apollo program director,

General Samuel Phillips,
found that the builder,

North American Aviation, had quality below
NASA's standards and deadlines that kept
slipping.
A quality inspector at the Cape,
Thomas Baron, went further.

He wrote a fifty-five page paper on
poor workmanship and safety violations,

and North American fired
him on 5 January 1967.
The company denied most of it,

though some company officials later testified
before Congress that about half of the
charges were well-grounded.
Those warnings lost to the schedule.

The Phillips report stayed
inside NASA until after the fire,

Baron was out of a job, and the program
was racing to reach the Moon before the end

of the decade, as President
Kennedy had promised.
The fire itself took less than a minute,

and what came next was a
five-minute fight to reach the crew.

At about 6:31 in the evening, a voice on
the radio reported a fire in the cockpit.

The pressure inside rose so fast
that the hatch could not be opened.
Seconds later, the capsule's wall split.

The pad crew fought through smoke
and heat to open all the hatches.

By then, nothing could be
done for the three men.

The review board found the most likely cause
was a spark from wiring near the floor,
close to Grissom's seat.
A Senate committee went further.

It said NASA's long run of success with
pure oxygen had led to overconfidence and
complacency.

NASA rebuilt the capsule with a hatch that
opened outward and a safer cabin air mix
on the pad.

In July 1969, Apollo
11 landed on the Moon.

The hardware was fixed, but that wasn't
the end of the complacency the Senate
described.

Some warnings come from
things that almost go wrong.

In April 1970, two days
into the flight to the Moon,
an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13.
The trouble had started on the ground.

The tank had been dropped about two
inches while it was being taken out of an
earlier spacecraft.

Later, in a ground test, its heaters ran
for about eight hours on sixty-five volts.

Its safety switches were
built for only twenty-eight.

That probably ruined them, and the review
board found that NASA and both companies

involved had missed the
mismatch in their paperwork.

The crew came home alive, using
the lunar module as a lifeboat,

and NASA called the mission
a successful failure.

But there was a problem
with an escape like that,

as the sociologist Diane
Vaughan later showed.

She studied Challenger and named what a
run of escapes does to an organization:
the normalization of deviance.

A problem turns up,
nothing terrible happens,
and slowly the problem becomes normal.

Each safe return makes the
next one easier to believe in.

The run of safe crewed flights after
Apollo 13 went on for almost sixteen years,
but it did not last.

By then, it was already happening
inside the space shuttle's boosters.

The shuttle's two solid rocket
boosters were built in sections,

and each joint was sealed by
two rubber rings called O-rings.

Hot gas was never supposed
to reach those rings.
On flight after flight, it did.

Rings came back scorched
and partly eaten away,
and the damage was accepted.

In January 1985, a shuttle launched
on the coldest morning so far,

and hot gas got past the first
ring in one of those joints.

Roger Boisjoly, an engineer
at the booster maker,

Morton Thiokol, found
that flight alarming.

That July, he wrote a memo to his
company's head of engineering.

If a joint failed, he warned, the result
would be a catastrophe of the highest
order, loss of human life.
The shuttle kept flying.
On 27 January

1986, the night before
Challenger was due to launch,

the forecast at the Cape
dropped below freezing.
Cold makes rubber stiff.
A stiff ring is slow to seal.
On a conference call that evening,

Thiokol's engineers recommended against
launching below fifty-three degrees

Fahrenheit, the temperature of the joints
on that cold flight a year earlier.
NASA's managers pushed back hard.
Thiokol went off the line to talk.

In that break, Boisjoly
later told the commission,

a senior manager asked the head of engineering
to take off his engineering hat and
put on his management hat.

When the call started again,
Thiokol recommended the launch.
The commission later found that NASA had,

in effect, asked its contractor to
prove it was not safe to launch,
rather than proving that it was safe.

The next morning, ice
covered the launch tower.

At 11:38, Challenger lifted
off in thirty-six degree air,

which the commission said was fifteen
degrees colder than any launch before it.

In the first second, smoke puffed from a
joint near the bottom of the right booster.
At about seventy-three seconds,
the shuttle broke apart.

Seven people were on board,
led by the commander,
Dick Scobee.
One of them was Christa McAuliffe,
a high school teacher from New Hampshire.

She had been picked from about eleven
thousand applicants to be the first teacher in

space, and children in classrooms
across America were watching.

At a televised hearing, the physicist
Richard Feynman clamped a piece of O-ring
rubber, dropped it in ice water,
and showed it no longer sprang back.

He wrote in the report that
for a successful technology,

reality must take precedence
over public relations,
for nature cannot be fooled.

NASA grounded the shuttle, redesigned the
joints and promised that it had changed.

Seventeen years later, the
pattern came back with foam.

The shuttle's orange fuel tank
was covered in foam insulation,

and pieces of it often
broke off during launch.

Early on, engineers saw
falling foam as a danger.

As the shuttles kept landing, it
came to be treated as routine.

In October 2002, a chunk came off the
same spot on the tank during the launch of

Atlantis and hit a ring
on one of its boosters.

It was the sixth known time
foam had come off that spot,

and managers chose not to
treat it as a flight problem.
Three months later, on 16 January
2003, Columbia lifted off.
About eighty-two seconds into the flight,

a piece of foam broke off the tank and
struck the front edge of the left wing.

Engineers spotted the strike on
the launch film the next day,

and wanted the military to
photograph the wing in orbit.

By the investigators' count, there
were three separate requests.
None of them went through.

Personal notes quoted by the board say the
request was dropped because even if they

saw something, they couldn't
do anything about it.
Engineers ran a computer model instead.

The board found they concluded from it
that there was no safety-of-flight issue.

The model had been checked against pieces
of debris of up to three cubic inches.

The board's best estimate was that Columbia's
foam was four hundred times bigger.

One engineer, Rodney Rocha, wrote an
email saying it was wrong not to ask for
outside help to get the pictures.

He reminded them of the NASA
safety posters that said,
if it's not safe, say so.
Then he wrote, yes, it's that serious.

He never sent it, because,
he told investigators,

he didn't want to go
over his managers' heads.
Mission Control did email the commander,

Rick Husband, and the
pilot, William McCool,
about the foam strike.

It told them there was
absolutely no concern for entry.
On 1 February,

as Columbia came home, hot gas
got in through the broken wing.

Over Texas, about sixteen
minutes before landing,

Columbia broke apart with
seven astronauts on board.
Among them were Kalpana Chawla,
who was born in India, and Ilan Ramon,
Israel's first astronaut.

That July, the investigators fired their
foam at a wing panel and made the hole from
the start of this video.

Their report said NASA's culture had as
much to do with the accident as the foam.

It called the repeating patterns
the echoes of Challenger.

All three disasters fell within six
days of each other on the calendar,

and every January, NASA remembers them
together on one Day of Remembrance.

The board also said why
the warnings kept losing.
In both Challenger and Columbia,

it said, engineers were asked to
prove that it was unsafe to fly,

instead of having to
prove that it was safe.

NASA, it wrote, had inverted
the burden of proof.

Add a schedule that had to be met
and a long run of safe returns,

and a warning had to win an
argument it was set up to lose.

After the first of the three, as flight
director Gene Kranz later recalled it,

he told his flight controllers to
write two words on their blackboards:
tough and competent.

Tough, he said, meant being forever
accountable for what they did,
and for what they failed to do.

He told them those words
would never be erased.
He said it in 1967.
Fourteen more astronauts were lost anyway,

and each time, someone inside
had already seen it coming.
